full_judgment:
3. The Rule is resisted by respondents 2-4 by filing affidavit-in-opposition. The case of the respondents in substance is that the complaint case was not maintainable either under section 25(1)(b) of the act or under section 24 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 on the ground of limitation and the petitioner being a seasonal employee (Temporary) worker under the respondent's Tobacco Re-drying Factory during the leaf buying season which starts in March and ends in August every year the petitioner was legally terminated and was paid 7 days' wages in lieu of notice and further pay for 23 days was offered which, however, the petitioner refused to accept and the money order returned undelivered. The respondents state that the petitioner was terminated simpliciter without any stigma for the lack of job and the termination having taken effect from June 15, 1982. The respondents' definite case was that on amendment of the petition of the complaint on May 31, 1983 there was a departure from the original case as made out in the grievance petition. 

 6. So far the limitation is concerned it appears from perusal of the judgment of the Labour Court that it relied upon the decision reported in 28 DLR 368 where in a complaint case the first part made an amendment to the complaint petition beyond the period of limitation of 30 days making out a different, case on different cause of action from that of grievance petition. In the cause as the amendment was made beyond the period of limitation of 30 days it was held that the case was barred by limitation. In the case the petitioner was terminated with effect from 15th June, 1982 due to lack of work and instituted the case on 10.5.83 within the period of limitation. But the Labour Court found that by seeking amendment on 15.5.1985 which was allowed on May 31, 1983 the petitioner made a departure from his original case for reinstatement on setting aside the order of termination by seeking re-employment under section 12 on the ground of his retrenchment and held the case was barred by limitation following the decision in the case of Management Board of AR Hawlader Jute Mills Ltd. vs. Chairman First Labour Court, Dhaka 28 DLR 368. Having had gone through the record of this case as well as the judgment of the Labour Court we have no reason to take a different view as expressed by the Labour Court on the point of limitation. Mr. Khalilur Rahman cited the decision in the case of Karim Jute Mills Ltd. vs. Chairman, Second Labour Court, Dhaka, 42 DLR 255. It held that unless the requirement of law under section 25(1)(b) is complied with institution of the complaint petition before the Labour Court fails. Mr. Khalilur Rahman also relying upon a recent (unreported) decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Pubali Bank vs. Chairman, First Labour Court, Dhaka and another (Civil Appeal No.27 of 1987 decided on June 13, 1991) contends that the Labour Court not being a civil Court was incompetent to accept the petition for amendment. In view of several conflicting decisions pronounced by different benches as to whether the Labour Court is a civil Court or not the point fell for consideration before the Appellate Division and in that case the point was set at rest after reviewing a large number of cases and on interpretation of sections 34 and clauses (a) to (d) of section 36 and other relevant provisions of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 and the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 the learned Judges came to the conclusion that the Labour Court acts as a civil Court for a limited purpose so far the procedural matter is concerned and 'it will not exercise the powers like those given in Order IX or Order XXXIX rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure which the civil Court may exercise in a suit...................'Therefore, on the strength of the aforesaid instructive judicial pronouncement we are of the view that where the Labour Court allows an application for amendment giving rise to an altogether different case from the case as made out in the grievance which requires adjudication of a new cause of action it acts without jurisdiction. The Labour Court can exercise its power so far as it relates to the procedural matter as enumerated in different clauses of section 36 as has been spelt out by the Appellate Division.
